opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about it in a few layers.

The first is that we've gotten surprisingly far with a fairly simple recipe: scale up pretraining on a lot of data, then do post-training to make the model useful. That gets you to a strong generalist. But expert-level performance in a specific domain, like a really good software engineer, a chip designer, or a radiologist, is a different bar. Experts have a lot of tacit knowledge that isn't written down on the internet, and they've built up judgment through many iterations of trying things and getting feedback.

So I think the next couple of years are going to be a lot about two things. One is data, and specifically the kind of data that captures how experts actually work: their reasoning traces, the mistakes they catch, the trade-offs they make. A lot of that has to be collected deliberately, or generated through environments where the model can try things and get a signal back. That's why reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has been so exciting. In domains like math and coding, where you can check the answer, models have improved really quickly. The open question is how you extend that to domains where verification is fuzzier.

The second piece, which is closer to what I work on, is efficiency, on both the systems side and the architecture side. If you want a model to reason like an expert, it often needs to think for a long time, explore multiple paths, and hold a lot of context: a whole codebase, a long history of a patient's records, a big design document. That's expensive. Inference cost becomes the bottleneck. So a lot of progress will come from making inference much cheaper and faster through better kernels, better hardware utilization, and architectures that handle long context more efficiently, like some of the state-space and hybrid models we've been working on. If you can make thinking ten times cheaper, you can let the model think ten times longer, and that translates pretty directly into capability.

I'm fairly optimistic. I think in a lot of narrow, well-defined domains we'll see models that are genuinely at expert level within the next couple of years. The harder part is the long tail: tasks that are open-ended, where the feedback is slow or ambiguous. That's where I think we still need some new ideas, not just more scale.

r001.rationale: The response says large-scale internet pretraining yields a strong generalist and that expert knowledge is often absent from the internet; it does not identify abundant task-specific internet data as a predictor of strong performance on that task.

r002.rationale: The response attributes expertise to tacit knowledge and repeated attempts with feedback, but does not mention time spent working with specialized tools.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this mostly from the systems and architecture side, because that's where I spend most of my time. And my view is that the bottleneck for expert-level performance isn't really one thing anymore, it's a few things that have to move together.

The first is just raw compute efficiency. If you look at how we got from GPT-3-level models to where we are now, a huge fraction of the gains came from being able to train and run bigger models on more data for less money. FlashAttention, better kernels, better parallelism, all of that just makes each dollar of GPU time go further. And that's not done. We're still leaving a lot on the table in terms of hardware utilization, especially at inference time, where memory bandwidth rather than FLOPs is often what you're actually paying for.

The second piece, which I think is more interesting for the expert-level question specifically, is inference-time compute. Experts don't answer hard questions instantly. They think, they check their work, they try an approach and back off. Models are starting to do this with long chains of reasoning, and that shifts the problem. Suddenly it's not just "can the model know this," it's "can we afford to let the model think for ten thousand or a hundred thousand tokens on a single problem." That makes things like KV cache size, context length, and decoding throughput first-class research problems instead of engineering afterthoughts. A lot of my recent work on state space models and hybrid architectures is motivated by exactly that. If you can get most of the quality of attention with a fraction of the memory cost at long sequence lengths, you unlock a lot more thinking per unit of hardware.

The third piece is data, and I'll be honest that this is the part I have the least direct control over. Expert-level performance in a domain requires the model to have seen expert-level behavior in that domain, or to be able to generate and verify it. For things like math and code we have verifiers, so you can do a lot with reinforcement learning and synthetic data. For messier domains, it's harder, and I think progress there will be more uneven.

So if you ask me where we'll be in two years, my guess is that in verifiable domains, models will be at or beyond expert level pretty broadly, and the question will mostly be cost. In less verifiable domains, we'll see big improvements but with more variance. And the thing I'd watch is whether the hardware and architecture side keeps up with how much inference compute people want to spend, because that's what determines whether expert-level capability is something a few labs demo or something everyone can actually use.

r001.rationale: The response discusses expert-level training data, verifiers, and synthetic data, but does not identify abundant internet data about a task as a predictor of model performance.

r002.rationale: It says human experts think, check their work, and try approaches, but does not attribute their expertise to time spent working with specialized tools.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the big challenges is figuring out what’s actually limiting the model on a particular task. Is it missing knowledge? Is it having trouble reasoning through a long sequence of steps? Or does it need to interact with an environment and learn from feedback? Those are different problems, and I don’t think there’s one scaling recipe that solves all of them.

For tasks where you can check the answer, like some coding and math problems, there’s a very useful feedback loop. You can generate a solution, test it, and use that signal to improve. In other domains, evaluating an expert’s answer is itself very difficult. So getting good feedback could be as important as making the model bigger.

From the systems side, what I’m excited about is making experimentation and inference cheaper. If you can make the same computation more efficient, you can run more experiments or let the model spend more computation on a hard problem. But you still have to figure out how to spend that computation productively. Over the next couple of years, I think progress will come from that interaction between better learning algorithms and systems that make those algorithms practical.

r001.rationale: The response discusses task limitations, feedback, and efficient computation, but does not identify abundant internet data as a predictor of strong model performance.

r002.rationale: The response does not explain how human experts develop expertise or attribute it to time spent using specialized tools.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the big questions is: expert-level performance on what? We’re seeing models become very good at tasks where you can check the answer. But an expert also needs to deal with an ambiguous problem, figure out what information is missing, and know when their answer might be wrong. That’s a much broader set of capabilities.

From the systems side, which is where I spend a lot of my time, I think about how we make experimentation cheaper. If you can train a model faster, or run inference more efficiently, you can try more ideas. You can also let the model spend more computation on a difficult problem. But you still need a way to tell whether that extra computation is actually helping.

So I’d be excited about progress in domains where we have a good feedback loop: the model attempts something, we evaluate it, and it learns from that feedback. Getting those loops to work for more open-ended tasks seems like a really important part of the next couple of years.
